text: But let me take the sting out of that list right now, because a lot of it sounds far more intimidating than it is. Here is a plain sentence for each of the words you just heard. You do not need to memorise any of this. You just need it to stop being frightening.

An agent is a language model that runs tools in a loop, until a goal is met. That is the whole definition, and we will earn it properly tomorrow. A sub agent is the same thing, spawned by another agent to go and do one narrower job and report back. That is how one instruction becomes a hundred small actions.

Context is everything the model can see at the moment it answers. Your instruction, the files it has read, what it said a minute ago, and the results of anything it ran. Memory is the part of that you deliberately keep between sessions, so it does not start from nothing every morning. Almost every failure you will hit in this program is really a context problem wearing a disguise.

Tools are the actions you allow it to take. Read a file, write a file, run a command, search the web. Without tools a model can only talk. With tools it can work. M C P is simply an agreed way to plug new tools in from outside, so that the same agent can reach your issue tracker, your database, or your design files without anyone writing custom glue for each one.

Skills are short written instructions that teach an agent how you want a particular job done, so you are not repeating yourself every time. Plugins bundle those up so a team can share them. Hooks are the opposite direction. They let you say, whenever this happens, automatically do that. Run the tests after every edit. Review the code before every commit.

Modes and permissions are about how much rope you hand over. At one end, the agent asks before it touches anything. At the other end, it does whatever it likes without stopping to ask, which people call yolo mode. Neither is right or wrong. Choosing correctly for the job in front of you is one of the real skills here, and we will spend a lot of time on it.

And workflows are the shapes you put around all of that. Plan first, then build. Build, then review, then test. Or set a long loop running and let it grade its own work for an hour while you do something else. Same tools, very different results, depending entirely on the shape you choose.
